verses.text: The men of Ephraim said to him, “Why have you treated us this way, that you didn’t call us when you went to fight with Midian?” They rebuked him sharply.
He said to them, “What have I now done in comparison with you? Isn’t the gleaning of the grapes of Ephraim better than the vintage of Abiezer?
God has delivered into your hand the princes of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb! What was I able to do in comparison with you?” Then their anger was abated toward him, when he had said that.
Gideon came to the Jordan, and passed over, he, and the three hundred men who were with him, faint, yet pursuing.
He said to the men of Succoth, “Please give loaves of bread to the people who follow me; for they are faint, and I am pursuing after Zebah and Zalmunna, the kings of Midian.”
The princes of Succoth said, “Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna now in your hand, that we should give bread to your army?”
Gideon said, “Therefore when Yahweh has delivered Zebah and Zalmunna into my hand, then I will tear your flesh with the thorns of the wilderness and with briers.”
He went up there to Penuel, and spoke to them in the same way; and the men of Penuel answered him as the men of Succoth had answered.
He spoke also to the men of Penuel, saying, “When I come again in peace, I will break down this tower.”

Now Zebah and Zalmunna were in Karkor, and their armies with them, about fifteen thousand men, all who were left of all the army of the children of the east; for there fell one hundred twenty thousand men who drew sword.
Gideon went up by the way of those who lived in tents on the east of Nobah and Jogbehah, and struck the army; for the army was secure.
Zebah and Zalmunna fled; and he pursued them. He took the two kings of Midian, Zebah and Zalmunna, and confused all the army.
Gideon the son of Joash returned from the battle from the ascent of Heres.
He caught a young man of the men of Succoth, and inquired of him: and he described for him the princes of Succoth, and its elders, seventy-seven men.

He came to the men of Succoth, and said, “See Zebah and Zalmunna, concerning whom you taunted me, saying, ‘Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna now in your hand, that we should give bread to your men who are weary?’”
He took the elders of the city, and thorns of the wilderness and briers, and with them he taught the men of Succoth.
He broke down the tower of Penuel, and killed the men of the city.
Then he said to Zebah and Zalmunna, “What kind of men were they whom you killed at Tabor?” They answered, “They were like you. Each one resembled the children of a king.”
He said, “They were my brothers, the sons of my mother. As Yahweh lives, if you had saved them alive, I would not kill you.”
He said to Jether his firstborn, “Get up, and kill them!” But the youth didn’t draw his sword; for he was afraid, because he was yet a youth.
Then Zebah and Zalmunna said, “Rise and fall on us; for as the man is, so is his strength.” Gideon arose, and killed Zebah and Zalmunna, and took the crescents that were on their camels’ necks.
Then the men of Israel said to Gideon, “Rule over us, both you, and your son, and your son’s son also; for you have saved us out of the hand of Midian.”
Gideon said to them, “I will not rule over you, neither shall my son rule over you. Yahweh shall rule over you.”
Gideon said to them, “I do have a request, that you would each give me the earrings of his plunder.” (For they had golden earrings, because they were Ishmaelites.)
They answered, “We will willingly give them.” They spread a garment, and every man threw the earrings of his plunder into it.

The weight of the golden earrings that he requested was one thousand and seven hundred shekels  of gold, besides the crescents, and the pendants, and the purple clothing that was on the kings of Midian, and besides the chains that were about their camels’ necks.
Gideon made an ephod out of it, and put it in Ophrah, his city. Then all Israel played the prostitute with it there; and it became a snare to Gideon, and to his house.
So Midian was subdued before the children of Israel, and they lifted up their heads no more. The land had rest forty years in the days of Gideon.
Jerubbaal the son of Joash went and lived in his own house.
Gideon had seventy sons conceived from his body, for he had many wives.
His concubine who was in Shechem also bore him a son, and he named him Abimelech.
Gideon the son of Joash died in a good old age, and was buried in the tomb of Joash his father, in Ophrah of the Abiezrites.
As soon as Gideon was dead, the children of Israel turned again, and played the prostitute following the Baals, and made Baal Berith their god.
The children of Israel didn’t remember Yahweh their God, who had delivered them out of the hand of all their enemies on every side;
neither did they show kindness to the house of Jerubbaal, that is, Gideon, according to all the goodness which he had shown to Israel.

footnotes.content: Ephraim's pride stings more than the enemy's sword. They demanded a seat at Gideon's victory, forgetting that the Lord gives honor as He wills. How often I've wanted credit for work the Spirit accomplished through other hands.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gideon answers with gentleness, not defensiveness. He compares Ephraim's victory—capturing two Midianite princes—to his own opening moves, as a gleaning exceeds the vintage. This is the language of reconciliation, not rivalry.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A gracious word turns away wrath. Gideon credits God's work and elevates Ephraim's role, and their anger dissolves. Sometimes the hardest victories are not on the battlefield but in the heart, where pride yields to truth.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Three hundred men cross the Jordan faint but pursuing. The Jordan marks a real boundary; they pursue into foreign land where Midian still fights. Exhaustion cannot stop those the Lord has set on a course.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gideon asks Succoth for bread—a simple need, honestly named. The men are faint, the kings still flee; provision is a measure of trust in the One who has already delivered the enemy into his hand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Succoth refuses to believe what the Lord has already done. They demand proof of a victory not yet visible, forgetting that faith trusts the word of a faithful servant. Fear masquerades as prudence.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gideon makes a grim promise: if the Lord delivers Zebah and Zalmunna, he will tear their flesh with thorns and briers. The vow is conditional, rooted in faith in God's promise, yet it speaks of a heart already hardening.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Penuel, another city east of the Jordan, receives the same request and the same refusal. These places—Succoth and Penuel—were real towns in Gad's territory; their cowardice is remembered in stone.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gideon repeats his threat. He speaks with the certainty of a man whom the Lord has empowered, yet the anger beneath the words grows louder. Even a vessel of God can let judgment curdle into vengeance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Zebah and Zalmunna camp at Karkor with fifteen thousand men remaining—one hundred twenty thousand had already fallen. The scale of their defeat testifies to the Lord's hand, yet they have not yet yielded or fled.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gideon takes a high road through the tents of the nomads—an unexpected path. He strikes the army while they rest, secure in their numbers. The Lord often uses surprise and humility over frontal strength.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The kings flee, but Gideon pursues them down and captures both. He scatters their army and wins a complete victory. Yet in that moment of triumph, seeds of a different kind of danger begin to germinate.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gideon returns from battle, descending from Heres. The place-name speaks of sun and light, and he comes bearing the light of victory. But a righteous judge must also bear the weight of justice done.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A young man of Succoth, captured and questioned, reveals the names of seventy-seven elders and princes. Gideon does not forget their betrayal; he begins to keep an account of those who refused to help.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gideon returns to Succoth and speaks directly to their taunting words—"Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna now in your hand?" He has become the living answer to their doubt. Now comes the reckoning they feared.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gideon takes the elders of Succoth and teaches them with thorns and briers—exactly as he promised. Justice done, yes, but a reader feels the edge turning from righteous to harsh. The instrument of God grows heavy in his hand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He breaks down Penuel's tower and kills the men of that city. The tower falls; the men fall. Gideon keeps both his promises, and in keeping them, something in him shifts. Judgment can consume the judge.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gideon asks Zebah and Zalmunna about men they killed at Tabor. They answer that these men resembled princes—tall, noble, kingly in bearing. In this small exchange, we sense personal grief beneath Gideon's authority.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "They were my brothers, the sons of my mother." Gideon's voice breaks. These were his own kin, slain by these kings. The oath he makes is not boastful but rooted in blood: as the Lord lives, they should have lived.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gideon calls his son Jether to strike the kings, but the boy is afraid—he is yet a youth and cannot find the courage to take life. So Gideon rises and does it himself. A father cannot always pass the burden to his son.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Zebah and Zalmunna ask Gideon to strike them himself, for "as the man is, so is his strength." They acknowledge his might. Gideon kills them both and takes the crescents from their camels' necks—spoils of a complete victory.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Israel begs Gideon to be king—him, his son, his grandson. They want a dynasty, a human anchor in the storm. But the tide turns here; power, once wielded, begins to whisper seductive lies.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gideon refuses: "Yahweh shall rule over you." A true word, yet his next request shows the refusal may have been more pride than piety. Even the godly can say yes words while meaning no ones in their hearts.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gideon asks for earrings from the plunder. He notes they are Ishmaelites' earrings—a detail that anchors the wealth to its foreign source. Yet asking for gold, even from his people, is asking to be honored in a way kingdoms reserve for their rulers.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Israel gives willingly, spreading a garment and heaping gold into it. They honor the judge as a king in all but name. The people's eagerness to give reveals their hunger for a visible center of power.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Seventeen hundred shekels of gold, plus crescents, pendants, purple clothing, and chains—a vast treasure. The weight is real; the burden it places on Gideon's soul grows heavier still. Gold accumulates, but so does temptation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gideon makes an ephod from the gold and places it in Ophrah. An ephod could be priestly garment or idol; here it becomes a snare. Israel begins to worship it, and Gideon's house becomes entangled with idolatry. The greatest danger to a leader is not defeat but the fruits of victory.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Midian is subdued, Israel's heads are lifted, and the land rests forty years. What God accomplished through Gideon was real and lasting. Yet the gift of peace, left in human hands, becomes a seed-bed for forgetting.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gideon returns to his own house. He is called Jerubbaal now—the name the Lord gave him. But returning home, he is still a man with human weaknesses, living among people who wish to make him more than human.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gideon had seventy sons from many wives. A judge who once threshed wheat in hiding now gathers a household like a king. Children born to honor and power often inherit only the temptation that felled their father.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: One concubine in Shechem bears him a son named Abimelech—"my father is king." The very name speaks of the spiritual sickness growing in Gideon's house. He never claimed the throne, yet his sons inherit the ambition to rule.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gideon dies in a good old age, buried in his father Joash's tomb. He lived long enough to see much, yet not so long as to see the full fruit of his apostasy. Mercy sometimes hides the deepest consequences from the one who planted them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: As soon as Gideon dies, Israel turns to Baal worship. Readers today hear an echo in how quickly God's people forget His works and return to idols—the same pattern, the same hunger for visible gods. Looking back from a longer road, I see how often the Lord's deliverances are followed by our swift forgetting.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Israel forgets Yahweh their God, the One who delivered them from all enemies. The victories won at such cost dissolve in the mist of a single generation. Amnesia of grace is the deepest ingratitude.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Israel shows no kindness to Gideon's house, forgetting all his goodness. A judge loses even the memory of his labor once the eye is turned away from the God who worked through him. Fickle favor teaches the faithful to seek the Lord's eye, not the crowd's.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
